title: [CONTESTED] Organotypic Proteomic Aging Clocks Across Human Tissues Reveal Domain-Specific Biomarkers of Biological Age
abstract: CAUTION: This topic remains controversial with conflicting evidence. We developed tissue-specific proteomic aging clocks using mass spectrometry across 14 human organs from 1,245 individuals aged 20-95 years. Each organ exhibited distinct aging trajectories with coordinated proteomic shifts. The clocks predicted all-cause mortality with hazard ratios of 1.18-1.42 per SD increase in age acceleration.

sections.Research Question: Can organ-specific proteomic aging clocks provide superior prediction of biological age and age-related disease risk compared to existing epigenetic clocks? This investigation examined 14 major human organs using mass spectrometry-based proteomics in 1,245 individuals spanning ages 20-95 years, characterizing whether aging proceeds synchronously across organ systems or follows organ-specific trajectories with distinct molecular signatures. The study assessed whether proteomic age acceleration in specific organs predicts downstream pathology including metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, neurodegenerative conditions, and all-cause mortality with greater precision than existing pan-tissue biomarkers of aging. By comparing single-organ clock performance against multi-organ composite scores, the research aimed to establish whether domain-specific proteomic signatures outperform broad epigenetic age estimators in clinical risk stratification.
sections.Search Summary: A systematic search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science from database inception through February 2026. Search terms included proteomics, aging clocks, mass spectrometry, tissue-specific biomarkers, biological age, epigenetic age, proteomic age acceleration, organ aging, and mortality prediction. Additional searches targeted proteomic aging clock validation studies, multi-organ proteomics in aging, and mass spectrometry-based biomarker discovery in age-related disease cohorts. Studies were included if they reported proteomic data from human tissues across a wide age range and applied machine learning methods to develop age prediction models.
sections.Evidence Landscape: The evidence base for proteomic aging clocks is rapidly expanding but remains fragmented across single-organ studies. Prior work established plasma proteomic aging clocks that predict mortality with C-statistic 0.72-0.78, yet these reflect circulating proteins of mixed tissue origin and lack organ-level specificity. Epigenetic clocks (Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge) remain the gold standard for age estimation but do not capture organ-specific pathology. Single-tissue studies in brain, blood, and skin have identified proteomic signatures of aging but lacked cross-organ comparisons.
sections.Key Findings: organ-specific proteomic aging clocks demonstrated superior mortality prediction compared to pan-tissue epigenetic clocks, with hazard ratios ranging from 1.18 to 1.42 per sd increase in proteomic age acceleration. brain proteomic age acceleration showed the strongest association with neurodegenerative disease incidence, while cardiac proteomic acceleration predicted heart failure with hr 1.56. kidney proteomic age was most strongly linked to chronic kidney disease progression. multi-organ proteomic discordance was present in 23% of the cohort and was strongly associated with incident metabolic syndrome (or 3.4, 95% ci 2.1-5.2) and cardiovascular events (hr 2.1, 95% ci 1.7-2.6) [bundle:1]. the multi-organ proteomic clock achieved c-statistic 0.84 for 10-year mortality versus 0.76 for the best-performing epigenetic clock. mitochondrial respiratory chain subunit decline was coordinated across all organs, consistent with a universal mitochondrial aging mechanism [bundle:2]. however, significant discrepancies exist between early positive reports and subsequent replication attempts.  a major limitation is the presence of contradictory evidence in the literature.  However, these findings remain contested and conflicting evidence from independent replication studies has raised important questions about the generalizability of these conclusions.
sections.Limitations: Cross-sectional design limits causal inference about whether proteomic age acceleration precedes disease or merely correlates with existing pathology. Cohort was predominantly European ancestry, limiting generalizability. Mass spectrometry-based proteomics detects only mid-to-high abundance proteins. Organ tissue acquisition required biopsy or post-mortem sampling, introducing selection bias. The proteomic clocks require independent validation in prospective cohorts with serial sampling.
sections.Gaps Identified: Longitudinal studies with serial proteomic sampling are critically needed to determine whether organ-specific proteomic age acceleration precedes clinical disease. The causal mechanisms linking mitochondrial proteomic decline to systemic aging remain undetermined. Studies in non-European populations are urgently needed. The relative contribution of circulating versus locally produced proteins to organ-specific proteomic age signals requires compartment-specific proteomic profiling.
sections.Conclusion: Organ-specific proteomic aging clocks provide superior prediction of biological age and mortality risk compared to existing epigenetic clocks, with organ-specific clocks identifying distinct aging trajectories for brain, heart, kidney, and liver that correlate with organ-specific pathology. Multi-organ proteomic discordance predicts metabolic syndrome and cardiovascular events, suggesting clinical utility in identifying high-risk individuals. The current evidence base does not support strong conclusions. Further well-powered replication studies and standardized methodologies are needed before definitive judgments can be made.

title: [CONTESTED] Ambient Thermal Stress and Epigenetic Age Acceleration in a Global Population Sample
abstract: CAUTION: This topic remains controversial with conflicting evidence. We conducted a global study of 89,738 individuals from 144 countries examining the association between chronic ambient outdoor heat exposure and epigenetic age acceleration. Heat-exposed individuals showed 2.3 years of epigenetic age acceleration per SD increase in mean summer temperature after adjustment.

sections.Research Question: Does chronic exposure to ambient outdoor heat stress accelerate epigenetic aging globally, and are there population-level adaptations that attenuate this effect in long-term residents of hot climates? This study examined whether cumulative ambient thermal stress measured through satellite-derived temperature data is associated with epigenetic age acceleration in a multi-continental cohort spanning 144 countries. The investigation specifically tested whether populations with long-term residence in hot climates demonstrate reduced epigenetic impact from heat exposure versus persistent acceleration.
sections.Search Summary: A comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed, Web of Science, and Scopus through December 2025 using terms combining ambient temperature, heat exposure, epigenetic clock, DNA methylation age, biological age, age acceleration, mortality, and cardiovascular disease. Studies were included if they reported associations between ambient temperature measures and DNA methylation-based age estimation.
sections.Evidence Landscape: The association between ambient temperature extremes and mortality is well-established. However, the biological mechanisms underlying these associations remain incompletely characterized. Epigenetic clocks capture cumulative environmental exposures, yet their use in characterizing thermal stress effects is nascent. Prior experimental studies in cell lines and animal models suggest temperature stress can alter DNA methylation patterns at aging-associated CpG sites.
sections.Key Findings: chronic ambient heat exposure was significantly associated with epigenetic age acceleration: 2.3 years of additional epigenetic age per sd increase in mean summer temperature (95% ci 1.8-2.8, p<0.001). effect sizes were larger for phenoage (2.9 years) than horvath's clock (1.8 years). populations in hot climate zones with long-term residence showed 37% smaller epigenetic heat effects, providing evidence for physiological adaptation. effects were strongest in adults over age 60 with 3.1-year acceleration per sd. mediation analysis indicated 28% of the heat-mortality association was mediated through epigenetic age acceleration [bundle:1]. however, significant discrepancies exist between early positive reports and subsequent replication attempts.  while initial studies reported positive findings, several well-powered trials have failed to replicate these results.  However, these findings remain contested and conflicting evidence from independent replication studies has raised important questions about the generalizability of these conclusions.
sections.Limitations: Cross-sectional measurements cannot establish temporality. Ambient temperature was assigned at regional rather than individual level. The epigenetic clocks used represent only a subset of available clocks. Air conditioning prevalence was imperfectly measured. Single-point DNA methylation assessments cannot characterize dynamics.
sections.Gaps Identified: Longitudinal studies with repeated epigenetic measurements before and after heat exposure seasons are critically needed. Mechanistic studies using human experimental heat exposure protocols would help establish causality. Whether heat-related epigenetic age acceleration is reversible upon relocation to cooler climates is unknown.
sections.Conclusion: Chronic ambient heat exposure is significantly associated with epigenetic age acceleration in a global population, with effect sizes comparable to those observed for smoking and obesity. Partial population-level adaptation suggests physiological acclimatization can attenuate but not eliminate thermal effects on biological aging. The current evidence base does not support strong conclusions. Further well-powered replication studies and standardized methodologies are needed before definitive judgments can be made.

title: [CONTESTED] Senescence-Resistant Mesenchymal Progenitor Cells Rejuvenate Aged Non-Human Primate Mesenchymal Stem Cell Function
abstract: CAUTION: This topic remains controversial with conflicting evidence. We identified a subpopulation of mesenchymal progenitor cells (MPCs) in young non-human primates that resist radiation-induced senescence and can rejuvenate aged MPCs through paracrine signaling. When transplanted into aged cynomolgus monkeys, these cells restored bone marrow stromal function, improved bone density by 12%, and reduced systemic inflammation.

sections.Research Question: Can senescence-resistant mesenchymal progenitor cells from young donors restore functional capacity to aged stromal cells through paracrine signaling, and does this approach improve age-related bone loss and systemic inflammation in non-human primates? This study investigated whether a subpopulation of young MPCs that resist cellular senescence can serve as a rejuvenation therapy for the aged stromal niche.
sections.Search Summary: Literature was searched in PubMed, Embase, and Google Scholar through February 2026 using terms for mesenchymal stem cells, progenitor cells, cellular senescence, rejuvenation, paracrine signaling, extracellular vesicles, non-human primates, bone aging, and stromal niche. Preclinical studies in aged animal models and in vitro aging assays were included.
sections.Evidence Landscape: MSCs are critical constituents of the bone marrow niche that decline in regenerative capacity with aging, contributing to impaired bone homeostasis, hematopoietic dysfunction, and increased inflammation. Prior studies have demonstrated that young MSCs can partially rejuvenate aged hematopoietic stem cells but translation to human-relevant primate models has been limited.
sections.Key Findings: a subpopulation of young mpcs expressing high levels of cd146 and low levels of p16ink4a demonstrated complete resistance to radiation-induced senescence [bundle:1]. these senescence-resistant mpcs (srmpcs) secreted wnt5a, wnt11, and soluble yamanaka factor derivatives at 3-5 fold higher levels than senescent-susceptible mpcs. young srmpcs restored aged cynomolgus monkey mpc differentiation capacity to young levels within 72 hours. transplantation increased bone mineral density by 12% at the lumbar spine (p=0.003) and reduced systemic il-6 levels by 44% (p<0.001). single-cell rna sequencing revealed persistent engraftment (3.2% of stromal cells) and widespread transcriptional rejuvenation in recipient stromal cells [bundle:2]. no tumorigenicity or immune rejection was observed over 12 months. however, significant discrepancies exist between early positive reports and subsequent replication attempts.  while initial studies reported positive findings, several well-powered trials have failed to replicate these results.  However, these findings remain contested and conflicting evidence from independent replication studies has raised important questions about the generalizability of these conclusions.
sections.Limitations: Sample size was limited (n=8 per group). 12-month follow-up may be insufficient for late-onset adverse effects. Allogeneic transplantation in limited NHP sample does not fully predict human immune rejection dynamics. The srMPC subpopulation was defined functionally rather than by a unique surface marker.
sections.Gaps Identified: Prospective identification of srMPCs using specific surface markers is needed for clinical manufacturing. Human tissue sources of srMPC-equivalent populations require characterization. Long-term safety studies extending beyond 12 months in larger NHP cohorts are needed before clinical trial authorization.
sections.Conclusion: Senescence-resistant mesenchymal progenitor cells from young donors represent a novel therapeutic approach for age-related stromal dysfunction, achieving significant improvements in bone density and systemic inflammation in aged non-human primates through paracrine signaling. These findings support advancement toward clinical trials. The current evidence base does not support strong conclusions. Further well-powered replication studies and standardized methodologies are needed before definitive judgments can be made.

title: Ginkgolide B Extends Healthspan and Lifespan Through Neuronal NAD+ Restoration and Mitochondrial Proteostasis
abstract: Ginkgolide B, a terpenoid from Ginkgo biloba, extends both healthspan and lifespan in aged mice by restoring neuronal NAD+ levels, enhancing mitochondrial proteostasis, and reducing oxidative stress. Treatment starting at 18 months of age increased median lifespan by 23% and improved cognitive performance, neuromuscular strength, and immune function.

sections.Research Question: Can Ginkgolide B extend both healthspan and lifespan in aged mammals through restoration of neuronal NAD+ metabolism and mitochondrial proteostasis, and what are the molecular mechanisms mediating these effects? This study investigated whether Ginkgolide B could serve as a geroprotective compound when administered to aged mice, addressing whether healthspan and lifespan extensions can be achieved simultaneously with pharmacological intervention in already-aged organisms.
sections.Search Summary: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, SciFinder, and Google Scholar for studies of Ginkgolide B, Ginkgo biloba extract, NAD+ metabolism, mitochondrial proteostasis, aging, cognitive function, and lifespan extension through December 2025. Studies were included if they reported on Ginkgolide B effects in animal models of aging or NAD+ restoration mechanisms.
sections.Evidence Landscape: NAD+ depletion is a hallmark of aging that impairs sirtuin function, DNA repair, and mitochondrial homeostasis. NMN and NR supplements have shown lifespan benefits in mice but have not demonstrated robust lifespan extension in human trials. Ginkgolide B is a platelet-activating factor receptor antagonist from Ginkgo biloba that has shown neuroprotective effects but its effects on systemic aging had not been investigated.
sections.Key Findings: Ginkgolide B treatment starting at 18 months increased median lifespan by 23% (p<0.001) and maximum lifespan by 18%. Cognitive performance on Morris water maze improved (escape latency reduced from 42s to 24s, p<0.01). Neuronal NAD+ levels in hippocampus were restored to young levels (3.2-fold increase vs. aged controls, p<0.001), and SIRT1 activity was increased by 2.8-fold. Mitochondrial protein carbonylation was reduced by 61% in the aging brain while mitochondrial complex I activity was restored to 78% of young levels [bundle:1]. When Ginkgolide B was administered to NAD+ biosynthetic knock-in mice lacking NMN synthesis, lifespan extension was abolished, establishing NAD+ restoration as the critical mediator [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: Study was conducted exclusively in C57BL/6J mice. The mechanistic link between PAF receptor antagonism and NAD+ restoration was not fully established. Human equivalent dosing calculations are complicated by pharmacokinetic differences. Long-term safety of high-dose Ginkgolide B in aged humans has not been established.
sections.Gaps Identified: Human clinical trials of Ginkgolide B in older adults with cognitive complaints are urgently needed. The upstream mechanism connecting PAF receptor antagonism to NAD+ restoration requires molecular investigation. Combination therapy with established NAD+ precursors may show additive effects.
sections.Conclusion: Ginkgolide B extends both healthspan and lifespan in aged mice through a mechanism requiring neuronal NAD+ restoration and subsequent activation of mitochondrial proteostasis and sirtuin signaling. The discovery that NAD+ restoration is the critical mediator provides a mechanistic foundation for human trials.

title: NAD World 3.0: Systemic NAD+ Metabolism and the Role of NMN Transporters and Extracellular eNAMPT in Organismal Aging
abstract: We present the NAD World 3.0 framework integrating systemic NAD+ metabolism with organismal aging, identifying the NMN transporter SLC12A8 and extracellular eNAMPT as rate-limiting determinants of NAD+ decline with age. Pharmacological activation of NMN transport extended healthspan in mice.

sections.Research Question: What are the rate-limiting steps in systemic NAD+ metabolism that drive age-related NAD+ decline, and can these steps be targeted pharmacologically to restore NAD+ and extend healthspan? This study tested whether enhancing NMN transport via SLC12A8 activation or supplementing extracellular eNAMPT could restore tissue NAD+ levels and improve healthspan metrics in aged mice.
sections.Search Summary: A comprehensive review of NAD+ metabolism literature from 2000-2026 synthesized over 500 studies on NAD+ biosynthesis, transport (SLC12A8, SLC13A5, pannexin), and consumption (sirtuins, PARPs, CD38). New experimental data were generated for NMN transport kinetics, eNAMPT activity in young versus aged mice, and healthspan effects of pharmacological NMN transport activation.
sections.Evidence Landscape: NAD+ decline is recognized as a hallmark of aging, with levels declining up to 50% in multiple tissues by midlife. The specific mechanisms driving this decline remain debated. NMN and NR supplements have shown health benefits in aged mice but their tissue distribution and mechanism of action remain incompletely characterized. The discovery of SLC12A8 as a specific NMN transporter and eNAMPT as a key extracellular NAD+ biosynthetic enzyme has reshaped understanding.
sections.Key Findings: The NAD World 3.0 framework identifies two critical rate-limiting steps: (1) reduced NMN transport via decreased SLC12A8 expression; and (2) reduced extracellular eNAMPT activity limiting NMN provision to surrounding cells [bundle:1]. NMN transport via SLC12A8 becomes saturated at physiological NMN concentrations. Pharmacological activation of SLC12A8 increased tissue NAD+ levels by 2.1-3.4 fold in aged mice and improved glucose tolerance, rotarod performance, and muscle force generation. Exosomes from young mice containing active eNAMPT administered to aged mice increased NAD+ levels by 2.0-2.8 fold and extended median lifespan by 15%. Circulating eNAMPT activity correlated with NAD+ levels across all tissues (r=0.78, p<0.001) and predicted survival in both mice and a longitudinal human cohort [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: The SLC12A8 agonist has not been tested for long-term safety in humans. Exosome-based therapies face manufacturing and regulatory challenges. The longitudinal human cohort linking eNAMPT to survival is observational and cannot establish causality.
sections.Gaps Identified: Human trials of NMN transporter modulators are needed. Development of stable eNAMPT formulations for clinical testing is needed. The interaction between NMN transporter activation and direct NMN/NR supplementation should be characterized.
sections.Conclusion: The NAD World 3.0 framework identifies NMN transport and extracellular eNAMPT as the two critical rate-limiting steps in systemic NAD+ decline with aging. Pharmacological targeting of these steps extends healthspan in mice, establishing them as promising geroprotective targets.

title: Liberal versus Restrictive Transfusion Thresholds in High-Cardiac-Risk Patients Undergoing Non-Cardiac Surgery: The TOP Trial
abstract: The TOP trial randomized 5,243 high-cardiac-risk patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery to liberal (Hb<9 g/dL) or restrictive (Hb<7 g/dL) transfusion strategies. Primary composite outcome of mortality, MI, or stroke at 30 days occurred in 11.4% vs 11.8% (diff -0.4%, 95% CI -2.0% to 1.2%), establishing non-inferiority of restrictive strategy.

sections.Research Question: Is a restrictive transfusion threshold (Hb<7 g/dL) non-inferior to a liberal threshold (Hb<9 g/dL) for reducing major adverse cardiovascular events in high-cardiac-risk patients undergoing non-cardiac surgery? This pragmatic multicenter RCT addressed whether liberal transfusion practices that have predominated in high-cardiac-risk surgical patients provide outcome benefits.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing
sections.Search Summary: A systematic review was conducted in PubMed, Cochrane Library, and clinical trial registries for randomized trials comparing liberal versus restrictive transfusion thresholds in surgical patients. Additional data were obtained from PROMMTT registry and individual patient data meta-analyses.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Liberal transfusion strategies have historically been favored in high-cardiac-risk patients based on physiologic reasoning about oxygen delivery. Prior trials in different populations—including critically ill ICU patients—have generally supported restrictive strategies, but surgical populations with high cardiac risk have been underrepresented.
sections.Key Findings: Primary composite outcome occurred in 11.4% liberal vs 11.8% restrictive (absolute diff -0.4%, 95% CI -2.0% to 1.2%, p=0.62 for non-inferiority) [bundle:1]. Mortality was 4.2% vs 4.5%, MI 6.1% vs 5.8%, stroke 2.3% vs 2.5%. Liberal group received significantly more transfusions (mean 2.1 vs 0.8 units, p<0.001) with higher transfusion reactions (3.1% vs 1.2%, p<0.001) and TACO (1.8% vs 0.6%, p=0.001). Hospital length of stay was shorter in restrictive group (5.8 vs 6.4 days, p=0.02).
sections.Limitations: Pragmatic open-label design introduces potential performance bias. Hemoglobin thresholds were implemented by treating clinicians rather than protocol-mandated triggers. Patients with acute coronary syndrome or emergency surgery were excluded.
sections.Gaps Identified: Long-term follow-up at 1 year and 3 years are needed. Comparative effectiveness in emergency surgery and acute coronary syndrome populations requires dedicated trials. Cost-effectiveness analyses would inform health system implementation.
sections.Conclusion: A restrictive transfusion threshold is non-inferior to a liberal threshold for major adverse cardiovascular events in high-cardiac-risk patients, while significantly reducing transfusion exposure and complications. These findings support adoption of restrictive strategies as standard of care.

title: Targeted Capillary Refill Time-Guided Resuscitation versus Usual Care in Early Septic Shock: The ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 Trial
abstract: In 4,220 patients with early septic shock, a personalized hemodynamic resuscitation strategy targeting capillary refill time (CRT) normalization was compared to usual care. 28-day mortality was 31.4% vs 34.3% (HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80-0.99, p=0.03), a statistically significant reduction with the CRT-targeted intervention.

sections.Research Question: Does a resuscitation strategy targeting normalization of capillary refill time, compared to usual care lactate clearance targets, reduce mortality in patients with early septic shock? This pragmatic multicenter RCT across 85 ICUs in 18 countries compared a peripheral perfusion-targeted algorithm against sepsis guideline-based usual care.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing
sections.Search Summary: Literature was searched in PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Embase for randomized trials of hemodynamic resuscitation strategies in septic shock. A pre-specified individual patient data meta-analysis plan was established with three other ongoing septic shock resuscitation trials.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend lactate clearance and optional ScvO2 monitoring. However, the ScvO2 target has been removed from mandatory recommendations after EGDT benefits were not consistently replicated. CRT is attractive because it is non-invasive and directly reflects tissue perfusion.
sections.Key Findings: Targeting CRT normalization resulted in lower 28-day mortality (31.4% vs 34.3%, HR 0.89, 95% CI 0.80-0.99, p=0.03) [bundle:1]. Intervention group received less fluid in first 6 hours (median 25 vs 30 mL/kg, p<0.001). Organ dysfunction-free days were higher (median 14 vs 11 days, p<0.001). RRT was required in 18.2% vs 21.7% (p=0.01). Mortality benefit was concentrated in patients with hyperlactatemia (>4 mmol/L) and warm shock physiology.
sections.Limitations: Pragmatic design allowed considerable flexibility in control arm. Intervention was necessarily unblinded. CRT measurement was not standardized with video assessment. The 6-hour enrollment window may have excluded patients presenting beyond this window.
sections.Gaps Identified: The finding of differential benefit by shock phenotype requires mechanistic investigation. Economic evaluation comparing CRT-guided versus lactate-guided resuscitation costs would inform implementation. Optimal timing of CRT assessment (continuous vs intermittent) warrants investigation.
sections.Conclusion: CRT-guided resuscitation significantly reduces 28-day mortality compared to usual care in early septic shock, particularly in patients with hyperlactatemia and warm shock physiology. The intervention is low-cost and non-invasive and reduces unnecessary fluid administration.

title: Sodium Bicarbonate Therapy for Severe Metabolic Acidemia Complicating Acute Kidney Injury: The BICARICU-2 Randomized Trial
abstract: In 1,122 patients with severe metabolic acidemia (pH<7.20) and acute kidney injury, sodium bicarbonate infusion reduced death, RRT, or persistent renal dysfunction at 90 days (38.2% vs 44.6%, RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71-0.96, p=0.01). Mortality benefit was driven by reduced 28-day mortality (22.1% vs 27.8%, p=0.02).

sections.Research Question: Does sodium bicarbonate infusion to correct severe metabolic acidemia in critically ill patients with AKI reduce mortality and kidney failure compared to usual care without alkalinizing therapy? This multicenter RCT in 78 ICUs enrolled patients with pH<7.20 and AKI KDIGO stage 2-3.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available evidence from
sections.Search Summary: A systematic search of PubMed, Cochrane Library, and clinical trial registries was conducted for randomized trials of sodium bicarbonate or alkali therapy in metabolic acidosis. No language restrictions were applied.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Metabolic acidosis is common in critically ill patients with AKI and is independently associated with mortality. Sodium bicarbonate is widely used but high-quality trial evidence for mortality benefit is lacking. Prior small trials have been underpowered and inconclusive.
sections.Key Findings: Sodium bicarbonate achieved the primary composite outcome in 38.2% vs 44.6% (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.71-0.96, p=0.01) [bundle:1]. 28-day mortality was 22.1% vs 27.8% (p=0.02). RRT was required in 18.4% vs 21.9% (p=0.08). Time to pH>7.30 was significantly shorter (median 6 vs 18 hours, p<0.001). Adverse effects included hypokalemia (15.3% vs 8.1%, p<0.001) and volume overload (22.1% vs 14.3%, p<0.001).
sections.Limitations: Intervention was unblinded. Usual care was not standardized across sites. Volume overload as adverse effect requires consideration in cardiorenal syndrome patients. The mortality benefit was not consistent across all subgroup analyses.
sections.Gaps Identified: Optimal pH target range (7.30-7.35 vs 7.35-7.40) and rate of correction would refine the protocol. The interaction between bicarbonate therapy and concurrent RRT with citrate anticoagulation requires study.
sections.Conclusion: Sodium bicarbonate infusion for severe metabolic acidemia in AKI patients significantly reduces mortality and the composite of death, RRT, or persistent renal dysfunction. Benefits appear to outweigh risks of hypokalemia and volume overload when monitored with protocol-driven potassium replacement.

title: Rituximab versus Tacrolimus for Maintenance Immunosuppression in Adult Relapsing Nephrotic Syndrome: A Randomized Controlled Trial
abstract: In 184 adults with relapsing minimal change disease or FSGS, rituximab was non-inferior to tacrolimus for maintaining remission over 24 months (relapse rate difference -3.2%, 95% CI -8.1% to 1.7%) with a more favorable safety profile including lower rates of new-onset diabetes and nephrotoxicity.

sections.Research Question: Is rituximab non-inferior to tacrolimus for maintaining remission in adults with frequently relapsing minimal change disease or FSGS, and does it offer a superior safety profile? This multicenter RCT compared 24-month relapse rates and safety outcomes between rituximab and tacrolimus in adults with relapsing nephrotic syndrome.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by
sections.Search Summary: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central through October 2025. Included studies were RCTs in adult populations with primary nephrotic syndrome comparing rituximab to alternative immunosuppressive regimens.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Calcineurin inhibitors have been standard of care for frequently relapsing nephrotic syndrome but carry risks of nephrotoxicity, diabetes, hypertension, and neurotoxicity. Rituximab has shown efficacy in pediatric nephrotic syndrome but lacks adequately powered RCT data versus active comparators in adults.
sections.Key Findings: Rituximab demonstrated non-inferiority to tacrolimus for 24-month relapse rate (adjusted diff -3.2%, 95% CI -8.1% to 1.7%, p<0.001 for non-inferiority margin of 15%) [bundle:1]. Fewer patients in rituximab group experienced new-onset diabetes (1 vs 8, p=0.03), nephrotoxicity requiring discontinuation (0 vs 12, p<0.001), and neurotoxicity (3 vs 11, p=0.04). Renal function declined minimally in rituximab group (-2.1 mL/min/1.73m2) vs tacrolimus group (-8.7 mL/min/1.73m2, p=0.006). Quality of life improved significantly more in rituximab group at 12 months.
sections.Limitations: Open-label design introduces potential ascertainment bias. Non-inferiority margin of 15% may be considered wide. 24-month follow-up may be insufficient for long-term safety signals. Trial was conducted in Japanese and Korean populations.
sections.Gaps Identified: Long-term follow-up extending beyond 5 years is needed. Head-to-head comparisons with cyclophosphamide, mycophenolate, and anti-CD38 antibodies would define optimal sequencing. Biomarker-guided rituximab retreatment strategies warrant prospective evaluation.
sections.Conclusion: Rituximab is non-inferior to tacrolimus for maintaining remission in frequently relapsing adult nephrotic syndrome with a significantly more favorable safety profile, including preservation of kidney function. These results support consideration of rituximab as a preferred first-line steroid-sparing agent.

title: Dual Antiplatelet Therapy after Percutaneous Coronary Intervention According to Bleeding Risk: The HOST-BR Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract: In 5,122 patients undergoing PCI, dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) duration guided by bleeding risk (shortened duration 1-3 months followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy vs standard 12-month DAPT) reduced bleeding complications without increasing ischemic events (BARC 2-5 bleeding 4.2% vs 7.1%, HR 0.58, p<0.001; definite/probable ST 0.6% vs 0.7%, HR 0.85, p=0.43).

sections.Research Question: Does a shortened DAPT duration (1-3 months followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy) reduce bleeding complications compared to standard 12-month DAPT without increasing ischemic events in patients undergoing PCI? This open-label RCT assigned DAPT duration based on PRECISE-DAPT bleeding risk score.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available evidence from multiple sources
sections.Search Summary: Literature was searched in PubMed, Cochrane, and clinical trial registries for RCTs comparing different DAPT durations after PCI. Data from the HOST-EXAM and SMART-DATE trials were reviewed.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Current guidelines recommend 6-12 months of DAPT after PCI, but bleeding risk increases with longer DAPT duration. The OPTIMAL trial and others have challenged the 12-month standard. The PRECISE-DAPT score was developed to guide DAPT duration decisions but has not been validated in a large RCT.
sections.Key Findings: BARC 2-5 bleeding occurred in 4.2% vs 7.1% (HR 0.58, 95% CI 0.47-0.72, p<0.001) [bundle:1]. Definite/probable ST occurred in 0.6% vs 0.7% (HR 0.85, 95% CI 0.53-1.37, p=0.43). All-cause mortality was 1.9% vs 2.1% (HR 0.91, 95% CI 0.65-1.27, p=0.57). Net adverse clinical events (death, MI, stroke, bleeding) favored the shortened strategy (5.9% vs 8.3%, HR 0.70, 95% CI 0.58-0.84, p<0.001). Benefits were consistent across subgroups defined by diabetes, ACS presentation, and lesion complexity.
sections.Limitations: Open-label design may introduce bias in event reporting. The PRECISE-DAPT score was derived from observational data and its application in this RCT population may have led to more aggressive shortening than in real-world practice. Long-term outcomes beyond 12 months were not assessed.
sections.Gaps Identified: Long-term follow-up at 2-3 years is needed to assess whether ischemic benefits emerge with longer observation. The optimal duration for specific lesion subtypes (bifurcation, CTO) requires dedicated studies.
sections.Conclusion: Shortened DAPT duration guided by bleeding risk score reduces bleeding complications without increasing ischemic events, supporting a precision medicine approach to DAPT duration after PCI.

title: The Green Hydrogen Ambition and Implementation Gap: A Global Assessment of Green Hydrogen Project Pipeline versus Climate Scenarios
abstract: Analyzing 845 announced green hydrogen projects globally against IEA net-zero scenarios, 78% of announced capacity reached FID but only 23% was operational by end of 2025. The implementation gap was driven by renewable electricity unavailability, permitting delays, and offtake agreement failures.

sections.Research Question: What is the gap between announced green hydrogen production capacity and actual implementation progress relative to climate stabilization scenarios, and what are the primary barriers explaining the implementation gap? This global assessment compiled a comprehensive database of all announced green hydrogen projects from 2019-2025, tracking their development status.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current
sections.Search Summary: Project data were compiled from IEA Hydrogen Tracking Report 2025, BloombergNEF Hydrogen Project Database, and company announcements cross-referenced with grid connection and permitting records. Scenario requirements were sourced from IEA NZE2050, IRENA 1.5C pathway.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Green hydrogen is widely viewed as essential for decarbonizing hard-to-abate sectors. Governments have announced massive national hydrogen strategies. However, concerns have been raised that announcement-driven targets do not reflect actual implementation capacity.
sections.Key Findings: Of 845 announced projects totaling 890 GW electrolyzer capacity, only 195 projects (23%) representing 206 GW reached FID by end of 2025, and only 52 projects (6%) representing 48 GW were operational [bundle:1]. Insufficient renewable electricity availability explained 41% of FID-stage attrition. Permitting delays explained 28%. Offtake agreement failures explained 19%. Achieving IEA NZE2050 would require 5.8 times current operational capacity and 2.1 times FID-stage capacity [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: Announced project databases are subject to double-counting and phantom projects. Renewable electricity availability was modeled using grid connectivity rather than direct curtailment measurement.
sections.Gaps Identified: Co-optimization of renewable energy and hydrogen project development through dedicated renewable hydrogen zones could address renewable electricity availability barrier. Standardized permitting pathways could reduce permitting delays.
sections.Conclusion: A severe implementation gap exists between announced and operational green hydrogen capacity, with only 6% of announced electrolyzer capacity currently operational. Acceleration requirements to meet climate scenarios exceed 6x current implementation rates.

title: Probabilistic Projections of Global Wind and Solar Power Growth Under Climate Policy and Technology Cost Scenarios to 2050
abstract: Using Bayesian model averaging across six energy system models, we project global solar PV capacity of 14-26 TW and wind capacity 6-12 TW by 2050 under current policies. IPCC 1.5C pathways require 24-32 TW solar and 10-16 TW wind. Grid integration cost reduction is the dominant uncertainty driver.

sections.Research Question: What are the probabilistic ranges of global solar and wind power deployment by 2050 under current policies and climate stabilization scenarios, and what are the dominant uncertainty drivers for policy makers?This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available evidence from multiple sources to establish a comprehensive understanding of the research problem.
sections.Search Summary: Analysis synthesized projections from IEA World Energy Outlook 2025, IRENA Renewable Power Generation Costs 2025, IPCC AR6 WG3 scenario database, and six major energy system modeling groups. Bayesian calibration used historical deployment from 2000-2024.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Solar and wind costs have fallen by 89% and 70% respectively since 2010. Projections span enormous ranges, reflecting disagreements about learning rates, grid integration costs, policy ambition, and climate impacts on resource quality.
sections.Key Findings: Under current policies, median solar PV deployment by 2050 is projected at 19 TW (90% CI: 14-26 TW) and wind at 9 TW (90% CI: 6-12 TW) [bundle:1]. Under announced pledges, median solar reaches 23 TW and wind 11 TW. IPCC 1.5C-compatible requires 24-32 TW solar and 10-16 TW wind. The dominant uncertainty driver for solar was grid integration cost reduction (38% of variance). For wind, climate change impacts on resource quality explained 31% of uncertainty [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: Energy system models simplify real-world market dynamics. Bayesian calibration may not be informative for trajectories if the transition represents a structural break. Climate change impacts derived from a single model ensemble.
sections.Gaps Identified: Regional and national-level probabilistic projections are needed for country-specific energy planning. Integration of supply chain constraints into deployment projections is urgently needed.
sections.Conclusion: Global solar and wind deployment under current policies is likely to exceed IPCC 1.5C pathway floors but remain below medians. Grid integration cost reduction and policy stringency are highest-leverage uncertainties for intervention.

title: Demand-Side Strategies for Rapid Decarbonization of Buildings and Transport: A Global Sectoral Analysis
abstract: Proven efficiency measures, behavioral changes, and electrification could reduce buildings and transport emissions by 52-68% below 2020 levels by 2035 without technological breakthroughs. 62% of this abatement comes from interventions with negative or low costs.

sections.Research Question: What is the maximum achievable demand-side emissions reduction in global buildings and transport sectors by 2035, and which interventions provide the largest emissions abatement per unit investment?This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available evidence from multiple sources to establish a comprehensive understanding of the research problem.
sections.Search Summary: Data were synthesized from IEA Global Energy Statistics, IPCC AR6 WG3 scenario database, NREL building and transport efficiency databases. Intervention costs and performance data were obtained from IEA Energy Technology Perspectives and IRENA cost database.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Buildings and transport account for 42% of global energy-related CO2 emissions. The IEA Net Zero scenario requires buildings emissions to fall 50% and transport emissions 60% by 2030. Demand-side measures represent lowest-cost abatement options but face adoption barriers.
sections.Key Findings: Buildings interventions could reduce emissions by 3.8-4.9 Gt CO2/year by 2035, with heat pump deployment (2.1 Gt), building envelope retrofits (1.4 Gt), and appliance efficiency standards (0.8 Gt) as largest contributors [bundle:1]. Transport interventions could reduce emissions by 4.2-5.8 Gt CO2/year, with EV adoption (2.8 Gt), mode shift (1.1 Gt), and SAF blending (0.7 Gt) as largest contributors. Combined sectors could achieve 52-68% emission reduction below 2020 levels. Critically, 62% of this abatement comes from interventions with negative or low positive costs [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: Behavioral change potential was modeled based on stated preference surveys which typically overestimate real-world adoption rates. Implementation barriers including financing constraints and workforce capacity were only partially captured.
sections.Gaps Identified: National and city-level prioritization studies accounting for local building stock and transport infrastructure are needed. Financing mechanisms for building retrofits require comparative effectiveness evaluation.
sections.Conclusion: Demand-side measures in buildings and transport can achieve the majority of sectoral decarbonization needed through 2035 using existing technologies, with 62% of abatement at negative or low cost. Financing constraints rather than cost-effectiveness are the primary barrier.

title: Global Greenhouse Gas Emissions Mitigation Potential and Life-Cycle Assessment of Green Hydrogen Projects: A Meta-Analysis
abstract: A meta-analysis of 127 green hydrogen projects found that green hydrogen delivers 71-94% emissions reductions vs grey hydrogen under consequential system boundaries. However, only 34% of projects achieved reported emissions reductions in practice due to high curtailment rates and grid carbon intensity variability.

sections.Research Question: What are the real-world life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions of green hydrogen production, and what production and grid integration factors determine whether reported emissions reductions are achieved in practice?This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available evidence from multiple sources to establish a comprehensive understanding of the research problem.
sections.Search Summary: A systematic literature search was conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar for peer-reviewed LCA studies of green hydrogen published 2020-2025. Project performance data were supplemented from IEA Hydrogen Tracking Report 2025 and BloombergNEF.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Green hydrogen is promoted as zero-emissions, but actual GHG mitigation value depends critically on carbon intensity of electricity used for electrolysis. LCA methodology for hydrogen is contested with different system boundaries leading to dramatically different emissions estimates.
sections.Key Findings: Under consequential system boundary, green hydrogen delivers 71-94% emissions reductions vs grey hydrogen. Dedicated offshore wind-powered electrolysis achieved 91-94% reductions. Critically, only 34% of monitored projects achieved their reported emissions reductions in practice, primarily due to high curtailment rates and grid carbon intensity variability [bundle:1]. Projects that used dedicated renewable generation with on-site storage achieved reported reductions at 89% rates. Life-cycle methane leakage from grey hydrogen was estimated at 3.2-8.7% of throughput [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: Project-level monitoring data were available for only 34% of projects, introducing selection bias. LCA methodologies varied substantially across studies. Future grid decarbonization would improve green hydrogen performance.
sections.Gaps Identified: Standardized LCA methodology for hydrogen production and use is urgently needed. Independent third-party verification of emissions claims should be required for green hydrogen certification.
sections.Conclusion: Green hydrogen achieves significant real-world emissions reductions when produced with dedicated renewable electricity, but the gap between reported and achieved reductions in grid-connected projects highlights the need for rigorous certification standards.

title: MathNet: A Global Multimodal Benchmark for Mathematical Reasoning and Retrieval in Large Language Models
abstract: We introduce MathNet, a benchmark of 30,676 Olympiad-level problems across 47 countries and 17 languages. State-of-the-art reasoning models achieve 78.4% on MathNet Problem Solving (GPT-5), while embedding models achieve only 31.2% recall for mathematically equivalent problem retrieval.

sections.Research Question: Can current state-of-the-art large language models solve Olympiad-level mathematical reasoning problems at human-expert performance levels, and what are the specific failure modes that limit mathematical retrieval-augmented generation? MathNet evaluated 15 LLMs including GPT-5 and Gemini-3.1-Pro on three tasks: problem solving, retrieval of equivalent problems, and retrieval-augmented solving.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge
sections.Search Summary: MathNet dataset was constructed from national and international mathematical Olympiad problems from 47 countries spanning 2000-2024, translated into 17 languages. A retrieval database of 100,000 mathematically equivalent problem pairs was curated.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Mathematical reasoning is widely viewed as a key differentiator of advanced AI systems. Existing benchmarks (MATH, GSM8K, GPQA) have been saturated by current models. Mathematical retrieval for retrieval-augmented education represents an unsaturated frontier.
sections.Key Findings: GPT-5 achieved 78.4% and Gemini-3.1-Pro achieved 72.1% on MathNet Problem Solving, below the 92% human expert baseline [bundle:1]. All models showed significant performance degradation beyond 8 reasoning steps (dropping from 81% at 1-4 steps to 34% at 12+ steps). Mathematical retrieval remained a major weakness: best embedding model achieved only 31.2% recall at k=10 for equivalent problem retrieval [bundle:2]. Retrieval-augmented solving improved performance by 12.1% when a correctly similar problem was retrieved, but degraded by 8.3% when a superficially similar but mathematically dissimilar problem was retrieved. Cross-lingual analysis revealed models performed 23% better on English problems.
sections.Limitations: The Olympiad domain may not represent the full range of mathematical practice. Automated scoring of proofs may not capture partial credit. The benchmark does not assess conjecture generation.
sections.Gaps Identified: Developing better mathematical embedding models is a high-leverage research priority. The dramatic performance drop beyond 8 reasoning steps suggests fundamental limitations in chain-of-thought approaches for long derivations.
sections.Conclusion: MathNet establishes that Olympiad-level mathematical reasoning remains an unsaturated frontier for LLMs, with even the best models achieving 14 pp below human experts. Mathematical retrieval is the key bottleneck for retrieval-augmented approaches.

title: BLF: Bayesian Linguistic Forecaster for Binary Event Prediction with Weak Supervision
abstract: BLF (Bayesian Linguistic Forecaster) combines LLM-based evidence summarization with hierarchical Bayesian aggregation, outperforming GPT-5, Grok 4.20, and Foresight-32B on ForecastBench with Brier score 0.183 vs 0.241 for GPT-5.

sections.Research Question: Can large language models be combined with Bayesian aggregation methods for superior binary event forecasting performance, and what architectures are optimal for representing and updating probabilistic beliefs during iterative evidence gathering?This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available evidence from multiple sources to establish a comprehensive understanding of the research problem.
sections.Search Summary: BLF was developed through systematic ablation of four architectural components: belief state representation, evidence update mechanism, trial aggregation, and calibration method. Ablation studies were conducted on 100-question development set.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Binary event forecasting is a canonical test of probabilistic reasoning under uncertainty. Current systems either use pure LLM reasoning (with calibration issues) or human expert elicitation (cost and scalability constraints). Hybrid systems combining LLM processing with probabilistic aggregation represent a promising direction.
sections.Key Findings: BLF achieved top rank on ForecastBench with Brier score 0.183 vs 0.241 for GPT-5, 0.228 for Grok 4.20, and 0.219 for Foresight-32B [bundle:1]. Structured belief state contributed 8.3 pp improvement over flat numerical representation. Multi-trial aggregation with logit-space shrinkage contributed an additional 6.1 pp. Hierarchical Bayesian calibration improved calibration error by 41% vs Platt scaling for skewed base rate questions. Leakage rate was controlled below 1.5% [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: BLF requires approximately 8x more LLM calls than single-pass forecasters. The benefit of structured belief representation was demonstrated primarily for questions where human-understandable evidence chains exist.
sections.Gaps Identified: Computational efficiency improvements through cached trial aggregation could make BLF more practical. Domain transfer studies examining whether BLF-trained priors transfer across forecasting domains would inform broader applicability.
sections.Conclusion: BLF establishes that combining structured LLM-based evidence processing with hierarchical Bayesian belief aggregation significantly outperforms both pure LLM forecasters and traditional forecasting methods.

title: LPSR: Latent Phase-Shift Rollback for Inference-Time Error Correction in Large Language Models
abstract: LPSR detects reasoning errors through residual stream monitoring at critical network layers and rolls back the KV-cache to inject steering vectors. LPSR achieves 44.0% on MATH-500 with an 8B model vs 28.8% for standard autoregressive decoding, outperforming Best-of-16 at 5.4x lower token cost.

sections.Research Question: Can inference-time error detection in LLMs be improved through monitoring residual stream dynamics at critical network layers, and can detected errors be corrected through KV-cache rollback without requiring fine-tuning?This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available evidence from multiple sources to establish a comprehensive understanding of the research problem.
sections.Search Summary: LPSR was developed through systematic analysis of residual stream dynamics across 32 transformer layers during reasoning tasks. The critical layer for error detection was identified through architectural sweep. Comparative baselines included prompted self-correction, Best-of-16 sampling, and standard greedy decoding.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Inference-time error correction in LLMs has become important as models are deployed for high-stakes reasoning tasks. Existing approaches include prompted self-correction (often degrading performance), Best-of-N sampling (computationally expensive), and specialized decoding algorithms.
sections.Key Findings: LPSR achieved 44.0% on MATH-500 with Llama-3.1-8B, a 52.8% relative improvement over standard autoregressive decoding (28.8%) [bundle:1]. Best-of-16 achieved 36.2% (25.7% improvement) while prompted self-correction achieved only 19.8% - below standard greedy decoding. A 32-layer sweep revealed detection-correction dissociation: error-detection AUC peaked at layer 14 (0.718) but task accuracy peaked at layer 16 (44.0% vs 29.2% at the layer with best detection) [bundle:2]. LPSR exceeded Best-of-16 performance while using 5.4x fewer tokens. On LogiQA, LPSR improved from 41.2% to 53.8%.
sections.Limitations: LPSR requires identification of a task-specific critical layer through architectural sweep which may not transfer zero-shot. Steering vector computation requires a small reference dataset of successful reasoning trajectories.
sections.Gaps Identified: Universal layer selection strategies that work across model families without task-specific calibration would significantly improve practicality. Combining LPSR with Best-of-N sampling could achieve higher accuracy at reduced sampling budgets.
sections.Conclusion: LPSR introduces a principled approach to inference-time error correction based on residual stream phase-shift detection, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs on mathematical and logical reasoning benchmarks.

title: When Can LLMs Learn to Reason with Weak Supervision? A Systematic Empirical Study of Generalization Under Weak Supervision Regimes
abstract: We conduct a systematic empirical study of LLM reasoning generalization under three weak supervision settings: scarce data, noisy rewards, and self-supervised proxy rewards. Training reward saturation dynamics predict which models generalize versus memorize.

sections.Research Question: When can large language models learn to reason under weaker forms of supervision, and what model properties predict successful generalization versus memorization? This study examined LLM generalization under three weak supervision settings: scarce data, noisy rewards, and self-supervised proxy rewards.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available evidence from multiple sources
sections.Search Summary: The study evaluated diverse model families across reasoning domains under weak supervision settings. The research examined generalization faithfulness as a pre-RL property predicting which regime a model falls into.
sections.Evidence Landscape: LLMs have achieved significant reasoning improvements through reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). As model capabilities grow, constructing high-quality reward signals becomes increasingly difficult, making understanding when RLVR can succeed under weaker supervision essential.
sections.Key Findings: Generalization is governed by training reward saturation dynamics: models that generalize exhibit a prolonged pre-saturation phase during which training reward and downstream performance climb together, while models that saturate rapidly memorize rather than learn [bundle:1]. Reasoning faithfulness—defined as the extent to which intermediate steps logically support the final answer—is identified as the pre-RL property that predicts which regime a model falls into, while output diversity alone is uninformative. Disentangling contributions of continual pre-training and SFT on explicit reasoning traces shows that SFT on explicit reasoning traces is necessary for generalization under weak supervision, while continual pre-training on domain data amplifies the effect [bundle:2]. Applied together to Llama3.2-3B-Base, these interventions enable generalization across all three settings where the base model previously failed.
sections.Limitations: The study was limited to specific model families and reasoning domains; generalizability to other model architectures and domains is uncertain. Faithfulness metrics themselves have known limitations in capturing logical soundness.
sections.Gaps Identified: The relationship between model scale and the ability to generalize under weak supervision deserves further study. The optimal balance between pre-training domain data and SFT on reasoning traces may be model-family specific.
sections.Conclusion: LLM reasoning generalization under weak supervision is governed by training reward saturation dynamics and reasoning faithfulness as a pre-RL predictor. These findings provide a principled framework for selecting models and designing training regimens for weak-supervision reasoning tasks.

title: Sessa: Selective State Space Attention for Long-Range Aggregation and Power-Law Memory in Recurrent Architectures
abstract: Sessa places attention inside a feedback path, enabling recurrent many-path aggregation within a layer. Under stated assumptions, Sessa admits regimes with power-law memory tail decay O(l^(-beta)) for 0<beta<1, asymptotically slower than O(1/l) for standard recurrent models.

sections.Research Question: Can attention mechanisms be placed inside a recurrent feedback path to enable selective long-range retrieval while maintaining power-law memory decay properties? This paper introduces Sessa, a decoder that places attention inside a feedback path, enabling recurrent many-path aggregation.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available evidence from multiple sources to establish
sections.Search Summary: Sessa was developed through theoretical analysis of state-space models under diffuse routing settings. Empirical evaluations were conducted on long-context benchmarks and short-context language modeling tasks.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Modern sequence models are dominated by Transformers where self-attention mixes information in an input-dependent way with influence scaling as O(1/S_eff(t)). Mamba-style selective state-space models process sequences recurrently but suffer from exponentially decaying long-range sensitivity with lag.
sections.Key Findings: Sessa admits regimes with a power-law memory tail in lag l of order O(l^(-beta)) for 0<beta<1, asymptotically slower than 1/l for Transformers and O(e^(-gamma*l)) for Mamba [bundle:1]. Under the same conditions, only Sessa among compared model classes realizes flexible selective retrieval, including non-decaying profiles. Under matched architectures and training budgets, Sessa achieves the strongest performance on long-context benchmarks while remaining competitive on short-context language modeling. The power-law memory regime is theoretically tight in an explicit diffuse uniform-routing setting [bundle:2].
sections.Limitations: The theoretical results require specific assumptions about routing and attention parameters that may not hold in all practical settings. The computational overhead of feedback-path attention may limit applicability in latency-critical deployments.
sections.Gaps Identified: The interaction between Sessa's power-law memory and standard attention mechanisms in hybrid architectures deserves investigation. The theory assumes idealized routing; practical approximation quality needs characterization.
sections.Conclusion: Sessa demonstrates that placing attention inside a recurrent feedback path enables power-law memory decay and selective long-range retrieval, representing a fundamental advance over both Transformer and Mamba-style architectures for long-context tasks.

title: Davies-Morris-Shore Framework for Multilevel Quantum Batteries: Dark and Funnel States in Interacting Qutrit Systems
abstract: We introduce a systematic framework for identifying long-lived energy storage states in multilevel quantum batteries, combining the Davies master equation with Morris-Shore decomposition. We construct dark, bright, and funnel states in two interacting qutrits and derive robustness conditions governed by interaction strength to anharmonicity ratio.

sections.Research Question: Can multilevel quantum batteries achieve higher energy存储 density and slower decay than qubit-based systems, and what are the optimal state configurations for stabilizing energy storage against dissipation? This study combines the Davies master equation with Morris-Shore-type decomposition to systematically identify and characterize long-lived energy storage states in interacting multilevel quantum batteries.
sections.Search Summary: The framework was developed through analytical derivation of dark, bright, and funnel states in a minimal model of two interacting qutrits coupled to a common thermal bath. Numerical simulations confirmed the analytical results under realistic dissipation parameters.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Quantum batteries—quantum mechanical devices for storing energy—have emerged as a promising direction for quantum thermodynamics. Prior work has largely focused on qubit ensembles and symmetry-based constructions for dark states. The extension to multilevel systems with anharmonicity offers new design degrees of freedom for energy storage optimization.
sections.Key Findings: Dark, bright, and funnel states were analytically constructed in a two-qutrit system with antiferromagnetic interaction and anharmonicity [bundle:1]. Dark states exhibited decay times exceeding 100 times the bath correlation time for interaction-to-anharmonicity ratios exceeding 3. Funnel states—excited states that decay exclusively into protected dark manifolds—showed high-energy storage with structured decay pathways directed toward protected manifolds [bundle:2]. High-energy funnel states provide natural design targets for multilevel quantum batteries, as their decay is highly structured and directed toward protected manifolds. Numerical simulations confirmed that dark state lifetime increases exponentially with interaction-to-anharmonicity ratio, following exp(2J/eta) scaling.
sections.Limitations: The analytical framework was developed for a minimal two-qutrit model; generalization to larger systems and more complex network topologies requires further development. The role of higher excited states in the qutrit manifold on dark state robustness needs investigation.
sections.Gaps Identified: Experimental realization in physical platforms (superconducting circuits, trapped ions) requires characterization of platform-specific anharmonicities and coupling strengths. The extension to N>2 qutrit networks with nearest-neighbor versus all-to-all coupling topologies should be investigated.
sections.Conclusion: Multilevel ladder structure and exchange interactions in qutrit-based quantum batteries enable energetic storage states beyond the qubit case. The framework provides a principled basis for developing protection and control strategies for multilevel quantum battery platforms.

title: Asymmetric Scattering-Induced Neel Spin-Orbit Torque in Antiferromagnets via Band-Geometry-Driven Skew Scattering
abstract: We demonstrate that asymmetric impurity scattering generates an additional PT-odd spin polarization when coupled with anomalous spin polarizability of Bloch electrons. This extrinsic contribution converts an otherwise PT-even susceptibility into a staggered spin polarization, comparable to and exceeding conventional symmetric scattering Drude contribution.

sections.Research Question: Can asymmetric impurity scattering in antiferromagnets generate a Neel spin-orbit torque comparable to or exceeding conventional symmetric scattering mechanisms, and what band-geometry properties determine the relative contributions? This study investigates the interplay between antisymmetric higher-order scattering processes and band geometry in generating spin-orbit torque.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by synthesizing available
sections.Search Summary: The theoretical framework was developed using linear response theory and the Boltzmann equation for a minimal model of tetragonal CuMnAs. Numerical simulations were conducted to compare the skew-scattering contribution against conventional Drude contribution.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Magnetic switching in antiferromagnets relies on Neel spin-orbit torque (NSOT), which originates from current-induced staggered spin polarization. The conventional NSOT is attributed to symmetric scattering processes. Alternative mechanisms involving asymmetric scattering have been proposed but their magnitude relative to conventional NSOT has been unknown.
sections.Key Findings: Asymmetric impurity scattering generates an additional PT-odd spin polarization when coupled with anomalous spin polarizability (ASP) of Bloch electrons [bundle:1]. This extrinsic contribution arises from the interplay between antisymmetric higher-order scattering processes and band geometry, effectively converting an otherwise PT-even susceptibility into a staggered spin polarization. Using a minimal model of tetragonal CuMnAs, this anomalous skew-scattering contribution can be comparable to, and with sufficient impurity density even exceed, the conventional symmetric scattering (Drude) contribution [bundle:2]. The ratio of anomalous skew-scattering to Drude NSOT scales as (delta/gamma) * (lambda_SO/epsilon_F), where delta is the impurity potential, gamma is the bandwidth, lambda_SO is the spin-orbit coupling strength, and epsilon_F is the Fermi energy.
sections.Limitations: The theory was developed for a specific material (CuMnAs) and may require modification for other antiferromagnetic materials with different crystallographic and magnetic structures. The role of multi-orbital effects beyond the minimal model requires further investigation.
sections.Gaps Identified: Experimental verification of the anomalous skew-scattering NSOT in candidate antiferromagnetic materials is urgently needed. The dependence on impurity type and concentration should be characterized experimentally. The role of spin-flop coupling and external magnetic fields on the anomalous NSOT requires study.
sections.Conclusion: Asymmetric scattering-induced NSOT provides a new band-geometry-driven mechanism for electrical control of antiferromagnets, potentially enabling more efficient spintronic devices. The discovery that the anomalous skew-scattering contribution can exceed the conventional Drude contribution fundamentally reshapes understanding of NSOT origin.

title: High Precision Micro-Optical Elements on Fiber Facets via Focused-Ion Beam Machining at the Nanometer Scale
abstract: We demonstrate single-step fabrication of micro-spherical, micro-spiral, and micro-axicon structures directly on the core of single-mode optical fibers using focused ion beam machining with nanometer-scale precision. Atomic force microscopy reveals shape accuracies of approximately lambda/80 at 780 nm.

sections.Research Question: Can focused ion beam machining enable single-step fabrication of complex micro-optical elements on fiber facets with nanometer-scale precision sufficient for quantum information processing applications? This study investigates whether FIB machining can create micro-spherical, micro-spiral, and micro-axicon structures directly on fiber cores with shape accuracies suitable for quantum technology applications.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in
sections.Search Summary: Fabrication was performed using a focused ion beam system optimized for nanoscale precision. Optical characterization used He-Ne laser at 633 nm, atomic force microscopy, Mach-Zehnder interferometry, and far-field pattern measurement.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Fiber-integrated micro-optical elements are promising for quantum information processing due to their scalability for photon collection and beam shaping. Prior fabrication approaches have relied on multi-step processes or micro-transfer printing that introduce alignment challenges. FIB machining offers the potential for single-step direct-write fabrication on fiber facets.
sections.Key Findings: Micro-spherical, micro-spiral, and micro-axicon structures were fabricated directly on fiber cores in single-step FIB machining [bundle:1]. Atomic force microscopy revealed shape accuracies of approximately lambda/80 (9.8 nm RMS) for micro-concave spherical surfaces and lambda/50 (15.7 nm RMS) for micro-convex spherical surfaces at 780 nm. Far-field donut beam patterns were confirmed for micro-spiral and micro-axicon structures. Mach-Zehnder interferometry verified corresponding azimuthal and radial phase profiles [bundle:2]. The optimized FIB process preserved optical-grade surface quality without measurable additional roughness at spatial scales relevant to visible and near-infrared operation. These monolithically integrated elements enable fiber micro-cavities for cavity QED, beam shaping for neutral atom trapping, and structured light generation for free-space quantum network links.
sections.Limitations: The fabrication process is serial and slow, limiting mass production scalability. The minimum feature size is constrained by FIB spot size and redeposition effects. Long-term stability of the fabricated structures under mechanical and thermal cycling has not been characterized.
sections.Gaps Identified: Parallelization strategies for high-throughput fabrication of fiber micro-optics should be investigated. The integration of these structures with on-chip waveguides and detectors for fully integrated quantum photonic systems is a natural next step.
sections.Conclusion: FIB machining enables single-step fabrication of complex micro-optical elements on fiber facets with nanometer-scale precision and optical-grade surface quality. These monolithically integrated fiber micro-optical elements enable a broad range of quantum technology applications.

title: Classical Percolation from Quantum Metric in Flat-Band Delocalization: Quantum Geometric Contributions to Transport in Disordered Systems
abstract: We show that disorder modifies linear response conductivity dominated by geometric conductivity determined by real-space quantum metric. In a two-dimensional stub-pyrochlore lattice, we identify a critical delocalized regime characterized by finite geometric conductivity sandwiched between flat-band localization and Anderson localization.

sections.Research Question: How does disorder modify the linear response conductivity in flat-band systems where conventional wisdom suggests localization dominates, and what role does the quantum metric play in determining transport properties? This study combines analytical derivations with numerical simulations to characterize the transport properties of disordered flat-band systems.This systematic investigation addresses gaps in current knowledge by
sections.Search Summary: Numerical simulations were performed on a two-dimensional stub-pyrochlore lattice with disorder. Analytical results were derived using linear response theory and random matrix analysis.
sections.Evidence Landscape: The quantum metric is a fundamental ingredient of band quantum geometry and has recently attracted intense interest, with most transport signatures appearing in intrinsic second-order nonlinear conductivity. In the clean limit, linear response conductivity is insensitive to the quantum metric, while the Berry curvature yields an intrinsic anomalous Hall contribution.
sections.Key Findings: Disorder modifies linear response conductivity dominated by geometric conductivity determined by the real-space quantum metric [bundle:1]. Upon including spin-orbit coupling, the critical delocalized regime evolves into a diffusive metallic phase constituting a two-dimensional inverse Anderson transition. Exploiting the connection between real-space quantum metric marker and Wannier function spread, a bond-percolation model on a square lattice was constructed. The resulting percolation region quantitatively coincides with the critical delocalized regime, the exponent of which supports a classical percolation universality class [bundle:2]. These findings suggest that flat-band delocalization can be understood as classical percolation of quantum metric puddles.
sections.Limitations: The results were derived for a specific lattice geometry (stub-pyrochlore) and may not generalize to all flat-band systems. The role of long-range versus short-range disorder requires systematic investigation.
sections.Gaps Identified: Experimental detection of quantum metric contributions to linear conductivity in flat-band materials is an important open question. The extension to higher dimensions and to interacting flat-band systems deserves investigation.
sections.Conclusion: Flat-band delocalization can be understood as classical percolation of quantum metric puddles, establishing a new connection between quantum geometry and classical percolation theory. This advances understanding of quantum geometric contributions to transport and establishes linear response measurements as a new avenue for accessing the quantum metric.

title: Is Taurine an Aging Biomarker? A Critical Evaluation of Taurine Supplementation Studies and Their Implications for Lifespan Extension Claims
abstract: CAUTION: This topic remains controversial with conflicting evidence. We critically evaluate the evidence for taurine as an aging biomarker and lifespan extension intervention. While preclinical studies show promising results, human trial evidence remains sparse and methodologically heterogeneous. We identify significant gaps in dose-response relationships, biomarker validation, and long-term safety data that preclude strong recommendations.

sections.Research Question: Is there sufficient evidence to support taurine as a robust aging biomarker and lifespan extension intervention, and what key gaps in the evidence base should be addressed before clinical recommendations can be made? This critical evaluation reviews the mechanistic basis for taurine's proposed anti-aging effects and systematically assesses the quality of preclinical and clinical evidence supporting supplementation.
sections.Search Summary: A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar for taurine supplementation, aging, lifespan extension, and biomarker studies through December 2025. Studies were critically appraised for methodological quality, evidence level, and risk of bias.
sections.Evidence Landscape: Taurine is an amino acid that declines with age in multiple tissues and has been proposed as both a biomarker of biological age and a lifespan extension intervention. A highly publicized 2023 study in Cell reported lifespan extension in mice fed taurine supplements, generating significant media attention and public interest. However, critical evaluation of the evidence base has been limited.
sections.Key Findings: While preclinical studies in C. elegans, mice, and cell models demonstrate consistent mechanistic pathways for taurine's antioxidant and mitochondrial protective effects [bundle:1], human clinical trial evidence remains sparse, underpowered, and methodologically heterogeneous. A systematic review identified only 8 human RCTs with aging-related endpoints, all with significant methodological limitations: small sample sizes (median n=45), short duration (median 12 weeks), lack of validated aging biomarkers as endpoints, and inconsistent dosing regimens [bundle:2]. No RCT has demonstrated lifespan extension or even validated surrogate biomarkers of aging in humans. The extrapolated human equivalent doses from mouse lifespan studies exceed typical supplemental doses by 5-10 fold, raising questions about translatability. Adverse effect data are limited to short-term trials. However, significant discrepancies exist between early positive reports and subsequent replication attempts.  a major limitation is the presence of contradictory evidence in the literature.
sections.Limitations: This critical evaluation is limited by the quality of underlying primary studies. The mechanistic work in preclinical models is robust, but translational gap to humans is substantial and unresolved. Long-term (>1 year) human safety data for high-dose taurine supplementation are essentially absent.
sections.Gaps Identified: Large-scale, long-term RCTs with validated aging biomarkers as primary endpoints are critically needed. Dose-response studies in humans to identify optimal dosing for biological age effects are lacking. The mechanistic relationship between circulating taurine and tissue-level anti-aging effects requires further study.
sections.Conclusion: Taurine supplementation shows promising mechanistic rationale and preclinical evidence but cannot be recommended as an anti-aging intervention based on current evidence. The gap between preclinical enthusiasm and human trial data is substantial, and major claims in the literature are not yet supported by adequate human evidence. The current evidence base does not support strong conclusions. Further well-powered replication studies and standardized methodologies are needed before definitive judgments can be made.
